nameStory: Stigeoclonium flagelliferum gets its scientific name from Greek words meaning "point branch" and "whip-bearing," referring to its branching structure that ends in long, whip-like extensions. This tiny freshwater algae doesn't have a widely-used common name, so scientists and nature enthusiasts typically just call it by its genus name, Stigeoclonium.
description: Stigeoclonium flagelliferum is a microscopic freshwater green algae that forms delicate, branching filaments in clean streams and ponds. While individual cells are invisible to the naked eye, colonies can form small, wispy green masses that look like tiny underwater cotton balls or green hair. These colonies are usually just a few millimeters across, though they can sometimes grow larger under ideal conditions. You'll need a magnifying glass or microscope to truly appreciate its intricate branching structure.

idTips.label: Branching pattern
idTips.description: Forms delicate, tree-like branches that feel incredibly soft and slimy when touched, with main stems that divide into smaller and smaller branches

idTips.label: Whip-like extensions
idTips.description: Branch tips extend into long, hair-like projections that wave gently in the current like tiny green whips

idTips.label: Colony texture
idTips.description: Feels extremely slippery and gelatinous between your fingers, like wet silk threads that immediately fall apart when lifted from water

idTips.label: Color and transparency
idTips.description: Bright green when healthy, often with a translucent quality that makes it appear almost glass-like in good light

idTips.label: Attachment style
idTips.description: Anchors to rocks, sticks, or other surfaces underwater with a small holdfast, but easily detaches with gentle pressure

idTips.label: Water preference
idTips.description: Only found in very clean, well-oxygenated water - acts as a natural indicator of good water quality

habitat: Look for Stigeoclonium flagelliferum in clean, cool streams, springs, and the shallow edges of unpolluted ponds throughout New England's forested areas. It prefers well-oxygenated water with some current, often attaching to rocks, fallen logs, or aquatic plants in partially shaded areas. This species is particularly fond of the clean mountain streams found in New England's higher elevations and serves as an indicator of excellent water quality.

seasonality.spring: Most active growth period as water temperatures rise and daylight increases. Look for fresh, bright green colonies forming on submerged surfaces in clean streams.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with largest, most visible colonies. May become less noticeable in very warm water or during drought conditions when water levels drop.
seasonality.fall: Still present but growth slows as temperatures cool. Colonies may appear smaller or more sparse as the algae prepares for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Greatly reduced or dormant in ice-covered waters, though may persist in areas with flowing water that doesn't freeze completely.

funFact: Stigeoclonium flagelliferum is so sensitive to water pollution that scientists use its presence as a living thermometer for ecosystem health - if you find this algae thriving in a stream, you can be confident the water is clean enough to drink!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other filamentous green algae like Cladophora, but Stigeoclonium's distinctive branching pattern that tapers to whip-like tips sets it apart. Remember: Stigeoclonium has a "Christmas tree" shape that gets thinner toward the tips, while Cladophora branches more irregularly without the characteristic whip-like extensions.
contextualKnowledge: This species is extremely rare in New England with only one documented observation, making any sighting scientifically valuable. The scarcity might reflect either the species' very specific habitat requirements or simply that few people look closely enough at microscopic freshwater algae to identify them properly.
compareHints: Stigeoclonium flagelliferum differs from its relative S. tenue primarily in its more robust branching structure and longer whip-like terminal extensions. While S. tenue forms more delicate, thread-like colonies, S. flagelliferum creates more substantial, tree-like structures that are easier to spot with the naked eye. Both species require very clean water, but S. flagelliferum tends to prefer slightly more turbulent conditions.
